newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bulldozers dig in, Arabs warn of violence.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bulldozers dig in, Arabs warn of violence.

text.p: Arabs on Wednesday warned of an outburst of violence and Israeli peace activists went to court to try to stop work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

While Israeli bulldozers ripped into the hilltop site for a second day, President Yasser Arafat's aide Ahmed Tibi told Israel Radio that Palestinian officials were doing all they could to prevent violence.

But he said: "No Palestinian can tell you what the reaction at any moment will be." He recalled the Palestinian uprising that erupted in 1987 was sparked by a road accident at a time of rage and frustration over Israel's occupation.
In Egypt, President Hosni Mubarak said Israel was leading the region into a new era of violence. Syria accused Netanyahu of bringing the region to the brink of war.
Tibi said he doubted Arafat would meet Israel's leader Benjamin Netanyahu so long as the construction went on.

"Mr Netanyahu's policy has killed the peace process. We're trying to defend this peace process (but) I don't think it's any more there," Faisal al-Husseini, the leading Palestinian in Jerusalem, told reporters after meeting foreign envoys.

Israel's High Court of Justice heard three legal challenges against the building of the 6,500 houses for Jews on the hill which Israelis call Har Homa and Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim. Israel Radio said the court rejected two of the petitions but were deliberating on the third.
Israeli forces remained on high alert for Palestinian violence in response to the project the PLO says violates peace accords with the Jewish state.

Netanyahu rejected international criticism of the settlement situated on land between Jerusalem and Bethlehem which Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war, saying it was part of the Jewish state's capital.
"I can't imagine any peace process under which we can't build in our capital," he told Israel Radio. "I don't agree to any peace that prevents us from building in Jerusalem."
Palestinians view East Jerusalem as their future capital.
About 200 Palestinians marched in the West Bank town of Ramallah in protest at the project. Palestinian police kept them away from Israeli roadblocks.

Last September, protests against Netanyahu's opening of an exit to an archeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem turned into gun battles that claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers.
Opinion polls published on Wednesday showed a majority of Israelis and Palestinians both favoured peace over conflict.
A poll of 479 Israelis in the newspaper Maariv found 60 percent supported the project while 26 percent opposed it.

But when asked whether they support the settlement "even at the price of international isolation and confrontation with the Palestinians," only 28 percent said they supported it -- 57 percent opposed it.
A poll of 1,542 Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip conducted between March 6-9 showed 56 percent believed the construction dispute must be resolved through negotiations.
The Centre for Palestine Research and Studies poll also showed that 65 percent of Palestinians were optimistic about the future despite tensions over Israeli plans.
The United States, Israel's closest ally, said on Tuesday peace efforts could be crushed by the Israeli project. Officials in Washington urged Israel and the Palestinians to resume talks.
The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) called for an immediate meeting of the United Nations Security Council to demand a halt to the settlement.

Netanyahu reiterated a charge denied by the Palestinians and the U.S. State Department that Arafat had given Islamic militants the green light to resume suicide attacks which killed scores of Israelis a year ago.
